snippet.title: Manager level roles: 12 questions you can expect during your interview
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

- First, let me define what I mean by “Manager level” - this usually means the role will be expected to manage employees, and people in general.

Telephone screen - 5 examples:
Have you had any major failures recently?
It is not uncommon to have a 45 minute call diving deeper exclusively on this topic.
How do you start your day? What is it that keeps you excited and going every day?
Motivation.
How do you prioritize workload?
Prioritization is something usually asked in more technical roles. At least this is what I learned.
How do you manage Managers and In-direct reports? How often do you communicate.
Management style. You could ask them this one too, especially in the onsite interview - and if they’re someone possibly part of your future team.
Tell me about one of your projects?
Your most representative project.

Onsite interview:
Tell me about a time when you fired someone
Tell me about a time when you set particularly challenging, yet achievable goals for your team
Tell me about a time when you encouraged a team member to take on a significant risk
Tell me about a time when you set a vision when there wasn’t one? How did you get buy in for this?
Tell me about a time when you felt like your team was not progressing quickly enough. Explain your approach, and the outcome.
Tell me about a time when you had to decide on whether to ask for additional resources for a project. What was the outcome?
Tell me about a time when you helped a team member to achieve a significant goal. What was the outcome?

One final note here, about how to answer these questions. It might sound tempting to always talk about success stories in these context, because, you know, that is quite natural, but, in my opinion, the main goal at this level is to advertise the right type of behavior; which basically means that you should use the most powerful possible story available to answer a question, instead of the more successful one - for example: if you’re asked, tell me about a time when you received negative feedback; the reflex would be to answer with a time when your boss didn’t get what you said, and you explained it and it was fine; an even better one would be when you were actually wrong, but still, you listened to their feedback and followed instructions to regain their trust. This could advertise the right type of behavior much better than if you’d say “they were wrong”.

So the overall idea is not to be afraid of talking about negative stories, if those are better to highlight on the behavior you’re interested to present - of course with the condition not to disqualify you from the job.

snippet.title: Technical roles: a simple indicator of a great candidate
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

- As you might expect, taking advice from a Romanian YouTuber, isn’t something that goes well in all cases
But this is not the main thing I wanted to talk about today; what I observed in some instances is, especially for people working in either technical roles, is that many of the answers are impossible to understand; and it’s not like the candidate doesn’t understand that I don’t understand, but they consider it irrelevant for me to understand the business logic, as they expect me to qualify their answer by the STAR format, or by how quickly they said it, or by how it ended on a positive note, or how quickly they came up with the story
What’s the issue with this? Clarity. Let me put it straight, a great answer begins with ensuring that your interviewer understands the sequence of events; this makes me relate to the leadership principles which Satya Nadella introduced at Microsoft - one of which is, they’re looking for candidates who Create Clarity.
So my point is, role play your answers with someone - anyone who it not from your field, and ask them - hey, did you understand everything that I said here? What do you think I could do to make it even easier for you to understand what I’m saying?

snippet.title: #1 Mistake prepping STAR Answers
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

- Does this failure story have anything to do with the job that you’re applying for? For example, if you’re a software architect, your failure should not be talking about how you failed a previous job interview, or how you were impolite to a coworker
Did your failure story get you fired from your last job? Or was it a similar type of mistake? Then you may want to use another one, unless you’re really confident it won’t disqualify you
Is your failure recent enough to be relevant? If you have 20 years in the workplace and you’re talking about how you screwed up your first task in a new role 15 years ago, that is a bit light for a failure

Can you quantify your failure? Doesn’t have to be money or time, but is this easy to understand? For example you failed a startup.

Do you have great learnings from your story? At least 3 of them?

Can you talk about your failure in an understandable way in 2 minutes or less?

When talking about your failure, did you spend half of the time for the situation, task and action, and the other half for the learnings?

Did you ensure that you’re talking about one single failure, not an enumeration of failures?

Are you being negative when talking about your learnings?

Is your language your normal language or is it scripted as if you’re making a speed in front of a thousand people?

Are you sure this is your best failure? It’s often I hear people change their minds after receiving some feedback?

note: I only scratched the surface with these filters :)

snippet.title: Who does well in job interviews
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

- False tracks:
1. They all prepare well in advance
2. They know the questions in advance
3. They speak well
4. They have a well crafted CV or they previously worked for a big business
5. They’re all nice people

a. They know exactly what they’re looking for, from the beginning
i. Hands on approach
ii. Could be they need just a confirmation of their knowledge or maybe they need help everyday until the interview, or they don’t need it at all; my recommendation would be to always know where you are and where you’re going
b. Do well under stress - They’re not quitters
 . this one is more widespread than you may think; many candidates understand what they have to do, but then they simply don’t deliver on it; it’s very frustrating and depressing, but it’s an all too common scenario; how do you not quit the prep process? Well, that’s easier said than done - as it’s very much linked with procrastination: https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20190805-eight-ways-to-curb-your-procrastination
i. Best people I know deliver, and deliver constantly, and are very hard to discourage
c. They focus on what matters to them
 . I am yet to find a successful candidate to tell me: Dan, I watched all your videos -  and by the way, they all find out about me because of my videos; 
d. They couldn’t care less about their English speaking skills
 . I once talked to a guy that I could only understand about 60% of what he was saying - I’m not joking; it was not a one-off thing, we met I think twice; you know why the guy got the job, this case at Amazon? Because of his attitude - he used to be a teacher in his home country - he knew the behavior will always trump artistic impression
e. They have many failure stories
 . I have to admit that I have not tested everyone that got hired for their failure stories, but the ones I did have at least a couple of high quality failure stories for their onsite interviews

snippet.title: Tell me about yourself - idea
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

- Just a super quick video here.

As I’ve been reading an interesting article - on CNBC from some well known executive recruiting agency.

And basically, the idea is to find some way to differentiate yourself from other candidates when answering this rather generic question “Tell me about yourself”.

Just a quick reminder here: what you want to avoid at all costs is to give a recital of your resume - that would be a super boring approach and will not play to your advantage.

So the idea is to find something unique, right, and what I recommend people is to take the following three elements into account:
Your core strengths - that are specific to your role
One or two highlights in your career from your CV

These would the the “standard way” that I recommend people to start crafting their own, engaging, answer to Tell me about yourself.

Another way to go about this, is instead of going with the professional highlights to mention an extraordinary achievement - the example in the article was: “I’ve climbed the highest mountains on every continent, including Everest.”

You may have different types of achievements, including winning some gaming tournaments -  especially if there is a little bit of team play involved.

So the point is to find that unique differentiator that represents you the most, even if it is not a professional achievement - the goal is to make it sound cool, and to ideally exhibit your strengths through it; in that example to climbing those mountains, that is a team effort, you can’t just go in all alone.

Last but not least, you’ll want to stay humble - and not go talking about that extra curricular achievement for 5 minutes straight. Work on the wording - it’s not an issue if that is communicated in one sentence. 

Expect follow-up questions - which will make the conversation evolve your way. I linked the article in the video description if you want to read it in full.

Thank you for watching.

snippet.title: 10 FAQs about creating the best possible CV
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

- 1. Does length of a CV really matter?
• Nope. What is the recommended length? I’ve seen people getting hired in super senior roles with a one pager, and others, such as SDEs with 5 pages in their CVs; think about the role you’re applying for and do your best to optimize for that specific audience
2. Do employers screen them using software in high performing companies?
• Yes. And they do it more often than you think; as you can apply for multiple roles these days for the same company
3. Do your chances to pass the resume screening round increase if you have a better looking CV?
• Yes. However, I am not aware of candidates getting hired because of this.
4. When does it make sense to have your CV beautified? Should you pay someone to do it for you?
• When you apply for a role that not only requires you to be an expert in the field, but also a leader
• Also, if the service is inexpensive, sure, why not - it will save you time
• Software that does it automatically: I am not aware of impressive results here, mainly because it is a wording matter, not a layout one
5. Is it important for your CV to be properly keyworded? Why?
• Software is used to parse applications, so you chances do increase, but not by as much as you’d think
• Recruiters reading CVs, because they read many CVs, tend to also look for keywords, so this might also play a role
6. Is it important that you tailor your CV for each application?
• Yes, so long as you don’t end up spending days on this; 
• I have seen successful applications because of this - however, this is not primary
7. What is the best structure for your CV?
• Depends on the role, and seniority, but as a general idea, I would have an intro, either including or followed by core competencies and then work experience, latest to oldest; hobbies could be included, especially if they touch upon core competencies required for the role, including gaming experience if appropriate
8. If I stopped working only just recently, and my original CV shows that I am currently employed, should I update my CV?
• Yes, you should have an updated copy, and bring it to the onsite, in case they want to ask you about it
• I wouldn’t recommend however going above and beyond to let them know I am currently unemployed
9. Should you mention references in your CV?
• Not mandatory, not many people do it; they can ask you for them - and they usually do after the onsite interview
10. Does an online profile, such as LinkedIn or personal website replace a CV?
• That could be interesting to manage your online presence and reputation, but keep in mind that more often than not, that is more of a liability - in the sense that if you do not update it, or it just looks bad, it can do more harm than good

snippet.title: How to pass a behavioral interview
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

- 1. Assess how much time you have to prepare, split that 50/50 writing and practice
2. What do you prepare - theory
a. Refresh your memory: Prepare stories for your most representative projects - junior roles could get away with 5, senior roles can have as many as 20 or more of these; some like to tie them to the principles of the company they’re applying for, such as for Amazon’s 14 LPs two of each;
• Greatest successes
• Failures
b. Prepare answers to questions
• Most commonly asked questions
• Tell me about yourself
• Why do you want to work here
• Failure stories
• If it’s for the onsite, then you’ll need to go one step further,
• If you expect to get grilled on behavioral questions
• Get a more tailored list to that specific company: I have a ton of lists on my channel, but you also can find them on Google - just don’t get too excited about the lists, that is mostly a motivational win
• Get the list with all possible ones
• Prepare answers - usually in writing; some like to prepare them on cards
• Best answers
• 1.5 minutes
• STAR format
• Quantifiable
• Bad answers
• Fail to communicate the story properly - you do not understand why they ask you the question
• E.g. a time when you received negative feedback from your boss - because they want to see if you can listen and eventually regain trust;
• Hypothetical situational
• Way too long - especially for people with consulting backgrounds 
• Do not memorize answers, you’ll get stuck and they sound scripted
• If it’s by phone, prep cheat sheets
3. Role-play
 . If you’ve never done this before: Find someone to role-play with and that someone must have a good understanding of these things
a. If you’ve done this before: 
• find someone to role-play with; or just speak the answers in the mirror until they sound great to you in the first place;
• Find someone to role-play with and to provide you with feedback too
b. Notes:
• Randomize questions
• It is not uncommon to role-play for two weeks
• If you find yourself using the same story over and over again, that’s a sign you don’t have enough of them
4. During the interview:
 . How long is the interview? To keep the level of energy
a. Cautiously optimistic
b. Do not block
c. If you don’t have an answer, repeat the question, ask follow-up questions, start talking about a hypothetical situation until a precise example comes to mind
d. Put together a great show

snippet.title: Does interview coaching work? Is it unfair to other candidates?
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

- This is so popular that companies such as Amazon even have automated weekly coaching sessions where people can ask questions. And this is besides them offering a one hour free coaching for important roles they’re hiring for.

It is unfair? Nope, 2 reasons:
1 MAybe the coach has insider knowledge: That might be the case, but my experience has shown this is not an indicator of success at all - I would even argue it is quite the opposite - people looking for insider info are more likely to spend too much time over this and eventually not prep the actual stuff enough
2 Maybe they have questions; Do not even think that sharing some questions is going to get you the job; and especially in the case of Amazon, there are hundreds of examples all over the internet, including on my YouTube channel

Myths:
1 I’d be very skeptical of coaches saying candidates who purchased a certain package, all got the job - no people, it never works this way, there is very little magic in this process
2 International candidates in particular are not able to prep properly because language barriers; When english is not your best language it is harder to find reliable information on search engines

Where is coaching useful
1 Busy people who have no idea or time to get used with the specificities - Amazon offers one hour free in case you didn't know; Mid to senior roles - where there is a lot of work to get the best possible stories; it is not uncommon to spend half an hour to tune up one answer or to decide on your best weakness
2 Role playing for hours does improve ones behavioral interviewing skills - in some cases significantly enough to get the job; just keep in mind this is an accelerator- i did not yet idex everyone who got an offer and thanked me, but I think it is above 50 people as of right now (if you’re curious, the most part are on my YouTube channel)
3 Building confidence and resilience to some extent, and ensuring you don’t suffer of confirmation bias

Maybe you have no idea about this, but, maybe you’ve worked with other routers - for which you have an answer, so at least you show them that you do know what they’re talking about and you could eventually convince them this command is just a Google search away
Remember that often times they ask you questions to see how you’d go about resolving a challenge - to see your approach:
Would you be someone they’d enjoy working with or someone that when they get asked “what’s the most innovative idea you’ve worked on recently” - thinks like “I would never spill the beans on this one, especially with you”
Do you have, or can easily acquire, the expertise to get the job done? As in my example with that router.
Do you have the toughness to get the job done? Or you’re just complacent and says “I have no idea, next question please”

1. Underestimate the time it takes to prepare
o The ones that got hired all spent an average of Two weeks prep
2. Prepare what matters
o Speakers practice speaking, technical ppl practice technical stuff
3. Language is not everything
4. Demotivate after failing once
o It is not a precise science - try again
o Or try multiple jobs, including at the same place, at the same time
5. Do not underestimate Confidence
o Best predictor of high performance, show it during the interview
o Not to confuse with confirmation bias
6. Do not spend the bulk of your time on the internet; don’t use it as a time sink; Journey Inside is broader than the one outside
o Reactive vs proactive
7. Be thankful realize this opportunity is important
o Helped hire grads on pretty much every continent
o My first interaction with hr in the us was in the pest control industry
o Many applicants that nobody would ever bother screening
8. Professional experiences are the projects that you’re the most proud of, ideally in a team context
o Solo projects are fine, but you’re not applying to start your own company
9. Take a look over the 36 most asked questions that I published in another video, that is a great starting point
o Don’t be surprised if it takes you two days to come up with an answer to just one question or two in the beginning
10. Find someone to Role play with
o It will not get you hired, but it will help you to better assess your readiness
o Don’t do role play for one hour; do it for two weeks straight

- When going in a job interview, your goal is to advance to the next stage.. And more often than not, your interviewer is like a gatekeeper - they want you to convince them that you could be the right candidate for the job.

How do you do that? Besides preparing the perfect answer to any question. The first thing you must do is to build rapport with that person. Rapport is when someone is totally responding to you - you feel like there’s a connection, and you understand each other well enough to be able to communicate effectively, and form a relationship.

Anthony Robbins: “Rapport is power” https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dENi7K2lX4U
Matching and mirroring. 

The challenge here is that most of us have a tendency to only bond well with people that are or act like us, or people who are like we want to be;

Even by phone:
Keep the same tone of the voice
The tempo
Keywords
Look at the wording in the CV

In person:
The posture
Mirror Eye contact - like them;
Gestures
Esp. when you say something important
Breathing
Proximity
Dont get too close
Shake hands
Firm or fishy

2. Misha Yurchenko «The STAR interview»
The pitch in the book is to become good at storytelling
Schedule the onsite interview after lunch.
Make eye contact every 3 seconds or so during the onsite.
Watch them in the eyes when speaking about drama: the company lost a million because of me.
Mirror the body language of the interviewer
Practice in a vacuum; at 5am in the morning or after midnight (harsh conditions to build resilience)

3. Misha Yurchenko «Cracking the amazon interview»
After the loop they gather in one room and decide if they should hire you or not
Positions above l5 get reference checked by the hr manager;
Print version is missing links - not much attention to detail

4. Dominic Black «Amazon Product Manager interview. Complete framework to succeed at your job interview and get hired as a Product Manager at Amazon»
Three things they are after when evaluating answers:
Fit: coworkers able to tolerate you
Motivation: if you will love this job
Strengths: whether or not you can do this job
Answering strengths with rule of threes
Strengths: analytical, leadership, see things through to the end
Weaknesses (some of them are better than others): bluntness, stubborn, unassertive, too negative, not focused on details, too confident, micromanager, distracted easily, too blunt, does not take feedback well, intimidating, impatient, unrealistic expectations, not a lot of confidence, short attention span, vague at times, overanalyzes, shy, cannot multitask, argumentative, doesn’t ask for help, procrastinates, indecisive (again, I have serious doubts of some being good ideas)
Prep method around 5 types of questions:
Leading and managing others
Difficult situations
Past failures and mistakes
Successes in your career
Working with others
3 stories for each of the 5 equals 15, to cover all 14 principles
Time preparing for the phone interview - 25-30 hours - half for the behavioral part
Time to prep onsite 60-70 hours, 25 behavioral
Men will want to wear a suit and tie
Own the room, show confidence

snippet.title: Amazon Interview: 33 Behavioral Questions For Project / Program Management Roles (Tech & Non-Tech)
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

Looking for someone to role-play before your interview? (free) https://amazoninterview.coach/role-play.php

- Amazon Interview Coaching: http://www.amazoninterview.coach/index.html#services In this video I give some hopefully useful advice for the behavioral part of the Amazon interview for Technical and Non-technical Project Management roles.

1. Describe a time when you went outside normal procedures to get a project done.
2. You are going to miss tomorrow's deadline, how do you and your team handle it?
3. Give me a detailed example of the project you have led before to help me understand more of your previous job.
4. What practical steps have you taken to elicit maximum contributions from each member of your team?
5. What is the most innovative thing that you have created?
6. In a situation where your intuition tells you there is a potential business opportunity, how do you go about finding the data necessary to substantiate it? Where do you even start?  
7. Tell us about your strengths
8. Describe a time that you exhibited leadership in your organization.
9. Tell me about a time when a decision you made didn't produce the results you wanted.
10. Tell me about a time when you disappointed a team member
11. Tell me about a time when you had to deal with a difficult customer
12. Give 3 examples of projects where you invented, simplified, delivered results quickly, and were able to scale to a larger result  
13. Tell me about a time when you proceeded to deal with an issue without your bosses OK.
14. Please tell me about a time when you had a project in trouble and how you handled it.
15. Tell me about a decision that did not go your way. How did you deal with it.
16. What was a challenge you faced during a project you worked on and how did you overcome it.
17. Describe a time you failed at work, or describe the most difficult situation you faced at work
18. When in your last job did you take a risk and fail?
19. How do you express different opinions to your manager?
20. Give me an example of when you have failed at a task, what did you do?
21. Tell me about a time when you innovated to simplify a process.
22. Talk about a project that you took with ambiguity (lack of data) and how did you proceed with the project?
23. Talk about a situation where you remotely influenced stakeholders and were able to get your work done. Explain the approach taken.
24. Talk about a project, where you had to take a difficult decision - Explain the decision, impact, reason for such decision, and how did you handle it, and the result?
25. Name a time you disagreed with your boss - how did the issue get solved?
26. How did you train one of your team members (Jr or Sr) to make him/her better in his/her daily work?
27. A time when you took a calculated risk, pushed through with it and succeeded.
28. A time when you used customer feedback to improve an aspect of your organization. 
29. A time when, halfway through a project, you encountered an incident/setback/roadblock and act to overcome it. With what result?
30. Give me 5 examples of how you are working to better yourself
31. Tell me about the most innovative thing you have ever created.
32. Name a time when you had to deal with a tough situation. Or, when you disagreed with management and what did you do.  
33. Tell me your most successful project which you led, what did you achieve at the end?

snippet.title: Tesla Interview (4 of 5): Example Questions & STAR Method
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

- They will ask you two types of questions: technical and behavioral. Now, for the technical roles, it is for everyone to basically know their thing - and maybe note that they might test your skills even during the screening interviews via a service named Codility.

But for the behavioral part, there are a few interesting aspects that can help you get through the process a lot easier.

First, the most common question they ask is: “Why Tesla?” so it’s always a good idea to prepare an answer here, and maybe keep in mind Tesla’s mission: “to accelerate the world's transition to sustainable energy” and the 4 things they look for in any candidate: being innovative, driven, collaborative and trustworthy.

All the other questions are pretty standard and easy to answer. 

Something you may want to prepare for in advance, as with any major job interview, is to develop more on the key stories in your resume. 

These can be explained using what is called the STAR method, for example, think of your most significant milestones in your career, such as your most successful project you worked on, or the least successful one, and then describe it using the STAR method: 
Situation - scenario
Tasks needed to get done
Actions you tool
And the result

As far as I’ve been researching, the main emphasis during the interview is on being technically fit to do the job - so you shouldn’t invest too much time into behavioral questioning techniques.

snippet.title: Tesla Interview (3 of 5): Interviewing Process
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

- The interviewing process is tailored for each position, but usually follows the following layout:
It starts with a phone interview with a recruiter - essentially the initial screening - with a preliminary conversation about the role. For technical roles there also might be an online test via a service such as Codility.

Then there may or may not be a second phone interview this time with either a hiring manager or someone more technical that has the main objective to determine if you’re worth an onsite interview.

For the onsite interview, you’ll likely be asked to prepare a presentation of a previous project you've done that is representative of your work. “Show, don’t tell” would probably be the best way to characterize this step. write and tell: Example in the video description)

Also, the onsite interview is run by a panel - that is a group of around 6 people - which is a great thing because it eliminates all sort of biases. 

After the panel presentation and Q&A - which generally take half an hour - there will be one on one discussions with members of the panel. You should expect mainly technical, job specific questions and some behavioral questions that I’ll exemplify later.

There could also be an extra phone interview - in case a key member of the panel couldn’t be present during the onsite interview.

For the technical questions - it seems that they got a bit harder in recent years, which is understandable given the scale and the reorganization of Tesla into functional units - from the traditional matrix style.

- These things were not that important when Tesla was small, but as a company grows, they have to obsess more and more about making sure their culture will be preserved - this is the same to pretty much any other highly successful business nowadays.

According to Tesla's head of global recruiting, there’s four main principles that are important at Tesla — being innovative, driven, collaborative, trustworthy.

This is the bread and butter of testing for cultural fit there, and you should really make sure that all your communication during the hiring process reflects these: from your CV, or the initial phone screening, to the project you have to present the panel, and the individual one on ones with the panelists.

snippet.title: Netflix Interview (2 of 3): Who they Hire, How to Apply & Resume Tips
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

- Netflix is looking for diverse people. And this is as straightforward as it gets at a top performing company where 80% of engineers are white and male. Regardless of the role, and despite the fact that they are becoming more and more a technology company. 

And this is essentially because they're expanding internationally and therefore having to adapt their offerings to their new audiences.

The other major trait that they look for in new recruits is ownership - and this is because, unlike at other major technology companies, Netflix has smaller teams with greater responsibilities. And when you have more responsibility it is likely to also have to know how to defend your decisions in real time as opposed to just responding to criticism during one on ones.

It is essential to not only appreciate the great recruitment marketing content in their culture deck but to also ask yourself if you would be a great fit there.

snippet.title: Netflix Interview (1 of 3): 2018 Culture Deck
snippet.description:
Netflix Culture Deck, in its 2018 format, explained.

1. Dream team
This is by far the most important of all and gives a pretty good idea of what Netflix is all about:

 “The unusual part is that we give adequate performers a generous severance package” so that we can find a star for that position”

Explain the dreamteam thing in para.

Interesting to note the difference between a team and a family:

“
We model ourselves on being a team, not a family. A family is about unconditional love, despite your siblings’ unusual behavior. A dream team is about pushing yourself to be the best teammate you can be, caring intensely about your teammates, and knowing that you may not be on the team forever.
“
Next, it describes various other Netflix policies, such as:
• The “keeper test”: 
“We focus on managers’ judgment through the “keeper test” for each of their people: if one of the members of the team was thinking of leaving for another firm, would the manager try hard to keep them from leaving? Those who do not pass the keeper test (i.e. their manager would not fight to keep them) are promptly and respectfully given a generous severance package so we can find someone for that position that makes us an even better dream team.”

• “Brilliant j****s.” 
“On a dream team, there are no “brilliant jerks.” The cost to teamwork is just too high. Our view is that brilliant people are also capable of decent human interactions, and we insist upon that. When highly capable people work together in a collaborative context, they inspire each other to be more creative, more productive and ultimately more successful as a team than they could be as a collection of individuals.”

And it closes with a pretty self-explanatory statement: “We s**k compared to how great we want to become.”

What’s here to learn as a candidate? Well, to me this is all about being a great team mate - and there is absolutely no formula for that - instead, the easiest way to be a bad team member is to act like a brilliant jerk, so the main takeaway for an applicant from this is to show generous amounts of humbleness during the interview.

2. Freedom and responsibility 
The main takeaway here is “the sense of ownership, responsibility and initiative so that this behavior [of doing the right thing to help the company at every juncture] comes naturally.”

Then again, the emphasis of people over process: “We believe that people thrive on being trusted, on freedom, and on being able to make a difference. So we foster freedom and empowerment wherever we can.”

The example of Reed Hastings gave: if you surround yourself with processes that people will have to follow you end up as an i***t.

Now what’s in for an applicant here? Ownership is a very sought after quality at Netflix as they give a lot more responsibility than other major tech companies. So to me a great investment of your time would be to prepare a story i. Which you took ownership over some problem situation or some event.

3. Informed captains 
4. Disagree openly

This one is a bit of continuation to the previous one which basically says that “Once the captain makes a decision, we expect everyone to help make it as successful as possible.” and that “Silent disagreement is unacceptable and unproductive.”

This one is quite interesting, it refers to how decisions at Netflix are being made. 

And they like to call this process to “farm for dissent” which essentially means that for every significant decision there is a responsible captain of the ship who makes a judgment call after sharing and digesting others’ views. 

That is as opposed to diffusing responsibility to a committee, because they believe in dissent - that is lack of agreement - as a fundamental means to make impactful decisions. 

For an applicant, of you are applying for a possible captain role - then this mainly refers to your abilities as critical thinking. As for the previous principle, a story that highlights your critical thinking skills is best thing to prepare here.

5. Context not control
Again, this basically refers to people over process. Interestingly they go as far as to give Steve Jobs as an example of being micromanager with some following that to new extremes of Nano managers. 

Needless to say Netflix is against micromanagement.

6. Highly aligned loosely coupled
This mainly refers to organizations getting too centralized a bureaucratic once they grow to a certain size.

The main takeaway here is that Netflix spends a lot of time on strategizing and then give their people the freedom to execute on their own tactics without prior approval.

7. Seeking excellence
And finally, seeking excellence contains Netflix commitment to not just maintain but to continuously improve on its culture, using its diverse workforce.

For an applicant, probably the best way to capitalize on these last two is to be sure to mention your strategic and execution skills towards excellence - usually through a story you may want to prepare.

snippet.title: Marriott Interview (1 of 3): The 5 Core Values
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

- This video is about Marriott's 5 Core Values.

Arne Sorenson talks about leadership and values. Knowing these 5 values will hopefully help you to build a better resume - maybe use some keywords too - as well as during the interviews, as you’ll know what the company stands for.

We put people first
Marriott’s end goal is to deliver a good experience to customers and this strategy was the same since they started. This is how they compete against everyone else for the loyalty of their customers and is the single most important value. The idea is, and I quote: “Take care of associates and they will take care of our customers.” 

So the main takeaway from this first value is they value very much people skills in their associates, and they are really good at spotting these things.

Simply put, for you as an applicant storytelling is the best way that you can make a good impression during the interview.

We pursue excellence
Excellence at Marriott refers to the ability to please all the various demographics of their customers. And at that level, that is mostly achieved through acquisitions other brands that specialize into evolving the culture of taste.

Why is this worth mentioning? Because think about alternative, cheaper,  way of achieving excellence: you try you fail you learn and then do it again - all this on the back of the customer. So the highlight here is in the approach.

As a candidate, I believe the main takeaway is to be sure that you emphasize you go above and beyond whatever your role may be.

We embrace change
Embracing change is about Marriott being actively interested in the latest technological advancements - they admit that the most innovation nowadays comes from the tech industry. 

Again, as for the pursuit of excellence, it doesn’t mean they are trying to copy AirBnB for example - they call it a different experience, however, they like being connected to the technological space - and in fact, the video featuring Arne Sorenson talking about values is one of the most viewed on my leadership series.

For an applicant, I believe the safest takeaway from this is open mindedness to new things or trends.

We act with integrity
Acting with integrity is probably best explained by a leadership trend that CEO Arne Sorenson talk about: people nowadays want to be respected because of their ideas. People want to work for teams that rewards them for their contribution in a personal way: they want to feel empowered to disagree, they want to see that their opinions matter, and essentially want to have an interest in making things better. This is in contrast with the past where there used to be a celebrity CEO that everyone had to follow. 

People can be successful leaders despite their different personalities. So I guess the main takeaway here is to be yourself, and be confident.

[smile]
We serve our world
“Sprint to serve” is as the name implies to be able to do it as well and fast as possible. And how they achieve it, given they work in so many cultures around the world, is that they decentralize as much as possible by empowering their local partners to come up with ideas. 

Ownership is a very important quality they’re likely looking for in any associate so be sure to highlight it in your CV and during the interviews.

snippet.title: Marriott Interview (3 of 3): STAR Interviewing Method & Examples of Interview Questions
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

Looking for someone to role-play before your interview? (free) https://amazoninterview.coach/role-play.php

- This video is about the STAR interviewing method, in Marriott's context.



First and foremost, there are tons of videos and training about the STAR method with many examples. I am not into spending too much time on the theory here, in fact you won’t see me giving any example STAR here - as I believe the one thing that matters most is to practice it.

Now before getting into the inevitable theoretical part, let me re-emphasize that, to me, Marriott is about creating good experiences. Inevitably therefore, an important part of any interview is to test one’s ability to communicate. What do I mean by ability to communicate? Storytelling.

Assessing one’s storytelling capabilities is not an easy thing - and this is also the main reason they usually prefer to thoroughly test this during an on-site interview. Now, I’ve heard applicants saying that they were asked to prepare a success story before the onsite, which is a bit light - only one story - if you want to properly prepare and invest the time needed to become good at these things.

But let's assume you only have to prepare one for now. It must be your career highlight - even if you don’t have one so far - you must highlight your greatest success in life so far. I’m sure you already have something in mind by now. 

Now take your time and write down everything about that event. Literally everything - it may take you 1 hour to do it, but it’s very important you think about it in the deepest detail possible.

Once you’ve done so, try to get specific on the following points:
• Briefly describe the situation you’re thinking about
• Mention allthe tasks that were needed to get done in that situation
• What action or actions did you take 
• And finally, what was the result of this situation

These 4 highlights will give you an answer in what’s called a STAR format; the situation, task, action and result. Before going further, keep in mind: you must sell yourself well - it’s very much about the experience here - so feel free to repeat - even in front of the mirror, and alter the composition of those 4 elements as you see fit, to allow you present your STAR in an enjoyable, needless to say positive, way. As a general rule here, if you’re not spending at least one hour with this, you’re either exceptional but most likely you’re acting superficial.

Now, why is it important to first think about the story and properly detail it, before summarizing it? That’s because you have a lot better chance to make it sound like a story, even if you have to summarize it into the STAR format.

Now, you may say, okay, but what is the point of structuring it this way - why not using another style to formulate an answer here? And the simplest reason is because Marriott calls such a story a STAR. Which is the obvious abbreviation of the method. Now this being said, so long as you cover these 4 elements, you should feel free to use your own format - if you're really good at these things.

And finally, make sure that you have at least 5 good stories that can be used in a wide range of contexts. Why? Because there are many flavors of behavioral questions, and the more stories you have prepared the better the probability you’ll be able to link them to a specific question.

Also, another method to prepare here is to take a look at the most common behavioral questions, and prepare one, two or even three answers for each.

It should go without saying, but the best possible way to prepare is to both have the 5 stories and to answer the most common behavioral questions. 

Practice is by far the best way to master this.

snippet.title: Google Interview (2 of 3): Googleyness, Example Behavioral Questions and the STAR Method
snippet.description:

Looking for someone to role-play before your interview? (free) https://amazoninterview.coach/role-play.php

- Two most important things in a recruit, behavioral questions and how to prepare (STAR method)

Now of course you have to be exceptional at the one thing that you’re applying for, but besides that, Google has to be very careful whom they hire is also a fit to its culture and teams which they call Googleyness. So like it or not, they must dive deeper into understanding how someone thinks so they can decide if the candidate is their best option here.
The first thing they measure here is cognitive ability, for example, they’ll ask you: Tell me about a tough problem you solved, how did you solve me, walk me through it.
Now, what’s the best way to prepare on these things? The best strategy I know is a two stage process: first, think about the highlight of your career, or something that you’re most proud of if you’re not there yet - think about it in the deepest detail possible - write it down even if it takes you an hour just for that. It is very important to do you best and have it done in a narrative format.
Once you’re done, get a summary - still, in a narrative format - not just some bullet points - and answer the following four questions:
• Describe the situation
• What are the tasks to accomplish
• Then talk about the actions that you took
• Results
This is what’s called to answer the question using the STAR format. The important bit here is to keep things in a narrative structure and to keep in mind Google’s cultural values here, remember the previous section in the video, for example:
• If you coded some website, be sure to highlight speed - 3. Fast is better than slow.
• Then if you worked on a team, be sure to highlight that there was communication going on and that you valued differences of opinion - 4. Democracy on the web works.
• Maybe you were in involved in a commercial project before, in which scenario a good pitch would be to highlight your motivation coming from a sense of higher purpose 6. You can make money without doing evil.
• Also, if you worked on something see if any of these keywords are representative: “passionate people from diverse backgrounds with creative approaches to work, play and life” 9. You can be serious without a suit.
• And finally, if you worked on some project for someone else (or you had a boss) be sure you mention how you went above and beyond to reach your goal - show customer obsession and thirst for excellence 10. Great just isn’t good enough.
Okay, so I believe these are the main highlights for what’s important when building your story. 
Once you have your first story, iterate 4 more time to get to around 5 stories of powerful moments in your career or life in general. One strategy here, when looking for topics for those stories, is to take a look at what are the most commonly asked behavioral questions during the interview, and take it from there - for example, the second story could be about dealing with failure, the third could be about a time when you had to deal with ambiguity, the fourth could be highlighting a time when you had a spark of creativity that contributed to reaching a goal a lot faster.
After you have the stories, the second step in preparing for the cognitive questions is to simply train yourself and answer, let’s say 20 such questions. And when I say answer, try to find more than one answer for each question - after all you have a good amount of information prepare from your main stories. Why multiple answers? Because the point is to impress your interviewer here and it’s possible your interviewer won’t like the first one, so it’s always best to have a backup plan - this one comes from Google itself.
Also, writing them down will help you get them to stick into your memory.
So this was my proposed approach on how to prepare to react to cognitive questions. But I believe this ability may help you throughout the application process, and even when building your resume.
Last but not least, if you remember there were two main things that Google looks for in a recruit - apart from the technical part, first was the cognitive ability and the second was leadership. The preparation for addressing this is embedded in the cognitive part I just talked about - that is to make sure you use Google’s keywords inside your stories.
But one more highlight here in terms of leadership - or at least one more interesting keyword - is emergent leadership. I noticed various Google HR leaders referencing it throughout the years; what does this mean: it’s essentially your ability to step in when there is a problem and step out when they are no longer needed. Would be great if you could also make this stand out in one of your prepared stories.

- Google prides itself for allocating resources to make sure that each and every resume is screened by a human being. 
This being said, this pre-screening step is also the one that weeds out the most applicants from the process. And not only that, but it’s basically your passport throughout the hiring process - your chance to make a good first impression.
Let me start with the obvious stuff:
Google takes applications serious, however, they receive more than a million each year. So no matter how well trained those people are, it is inevitable that they move fast. After all their principles apply to themselves, too, remember? 3. Fast is better than slow.
Now according to some statistics, a recruiter spends an average of just 6 seconds to go over a resume - this may not be the specific case at Google, but regardless, this is an interesting exercise: go ahead and read your CV in 6 seconds. Would you hire yourself based on the infromation that you’ve accumulated based on the first 6 seconds of your CV?
The structure of your CV should be the following:
• Start with your education 
• Work experience - reverse chronological order
• Project work
• Awards / leadership experience
• extracurricular
Recruiters at Google say one of the biggest mistakes on resumes is to poorly state accomplishments, for example, don’t just say: I grew sales by 20%, you should try to frame it like: I accomplished X as measured by Y by doing Z
Next, Google allows cover letters - which is another great way to make a good impression. Here are two examples that I liked the most: 
Cover Letters examples:
http://www.vault.com/blog/resumes-cover-letters/sample-cover-letter-to-a-google-recruiter 
And last but not least, and this should go without saying, typos in your resume won’t probably disqualify you, but you can be sure they will have a negative impact, so be sure you triple check it and ideally as a friend to review it for you.
Best way to pass the screening round; hiring process

The best way to increase your chances to get a job at Google is by getting a Googler to refer you. I’ve heard Google has some internal rule to have someone call you within 48hours if someone there refers you.
Okay, this may not be for everyone, but if there is the slightest chance you could have someone do it, it’s by far the most efficient approach.
Second, no matter how good looking and well-structured a career website is, applying through it is a passive experience. You apply, someone reviews your resume, as they also do for a million other people, and if, IF, they think you’re good then you’ll get to the next stage. 


What if you just cold called your hiring manager? Or let’s say you don’t have a preference but you cold called 4 hiring managers and be clear of what you want? Your chances will exponentially increase if you do so. And in fact many successful Googlers have done it in the past.
And the final tip I have here is that even if Google is reportedly saying they don’t require a cover letter, so long as they allow it, why not use it as a pitch? 
The hiring process at Google is very well explained on its website - so probably the best piece of advice I can give you here is to know that Google is well known for pioneering structured interviews, and being open about it. 
Why does this matter? Well it does because they’re between the very few to use quantifiable evaluation methods throughout the hiring process. A hiring committee uses an aggregate of these rankings to come to a final decision, while also taking other factors into consideration.
So the process, regardless of position is
• Application
• Screened
• If qualified
• Phone screen
• Onsite interview
• Decision is by committee

snippet.description:

- Facebook’s main interviewing strategy is to focus on alignment with their five core values, which I believe deserve a bit of explaining:

“Give people the power to build community and bring the world closer together.”

1. Be Bold: Building great things means taking risks. We have a saying: “The riskiest thing is to take no risks.” In a world that’s changing so quickly, you’re guaranteed to fail if you don’t take any risks. We encourage everyone to make bold decisions, even if that means being wrong some of the time.

Probably the best way to explain this is by reading Facebook’s story - which is basically that this is not by far Mark Zuckerberg’s first project and not even the first social network that he was involved in. And as he once said, if he knew what it meant to connect that many people, he would have never started Facebook.

Another major risk that Mark Zuckerberg took was a few years after Facebook started to grwo and when larger companies expressed interest in buying the social network - almost every senior executive quit Facebook because Mark Zuckerberg didn’t want to sell - he wanted to connect more people.

So I believe this should give you a good idea of what they mean by making bold decisions and how you can eventually embed a story of your own while preparing for an interview there.

2. Focus on Impact: To have the biggest impact, we need to focus on solving the most important problems. It sounds simple, but most companies do this poorly and waste a lot of time. We expect everyone at Facebook to be good at finding the biggest problems to work on.

One way to explain this is by referencing Mark Zuckerberg’s 2017 commencement speech at Harvard in which he started by saying that our generation will have to take on big bets to solve the problem of tens of millions of jobs to be be lost to automation. 

The idea here is be someone that gets excited about working on something with a higher purpose. You have to really buy into this type of thinking, if you want to do good there.

3. Move Fast: Moving fast enables us to build more things and learn faster. We’re less afraid of making mistakes than we are of losing opportunities by moving too slowly. We are a culture of builders, the power is in your hands.

This one is best explained by Sheryl Sandberg in an older interview, when she highlights one of the biggest differences between Facebook and Google. Google is great at AI, which is investing time to research stuff and then eventually roll it out in a staged approach. At Facebook by contrast, they ship features fast and check if they work, immediately. This is of course something they do with a small sample of their user base.

4. Be Open: We believe that a more open world is a better world. The same goes for our company. Informed people make better decisions and have a greater impact, which is why we work hard to make sure everyone at Facebook has access to as much information about the company as possible.
+
5. Build Social Value: Facebook was created to make the world more open and connected, not just to build a company. We expect everyone at Facebook to focus every day on how to build real value for the world in everything they do.

The interesting bit of this is the “not just to build a company” because Mark Zuckerberg doesn’t believe in the idea of starting a company and then finding problems to solve; he things it should be the other way around, and in fact, he reportedly said that Facebook was never meant to be a company in the early beginnings.

Again the main takeaway here is that people at Facebook should be motivated by a higher purpose - problem that has to be solved.

snippet.title: Facebook Interview (3 of 3): Example Behavioral Questions & The STAR Method
snippet.description:

- For the technical part of the interview, best way is to just ask your recruiter about it - because more often than not, they’ll already have some PDF with all the specifics.

Next I’ll be focusing on the behavioral side of the interview, where the goal is to evaluate if they would like to work with you in a team, your motivation, empathy and perseverance.

How can you assess these things? Well it’s of course by asking questions - behavioral ones, such as: How do you handle a difficult co-worker? Or How do you strive for success and growth?

While these look as simple questions, keep in mind you’re interviewing at one of the top companies in the world, so, there must be something special about you - something that will allow some sort of differentiation between you and other candidates.

How do you do that? One of the best methods I know is to prepare very well on a few stories, highlights in your life. For example, think about the most successful project you’ve ever had in your life, and try to remember as much detail about it as possible. If you don’t have one that’s particularly successful, think about your greatest failure so far.

[smile]
Once you’ve done so, frame it unde the following template:
Start by describing the situation - the genesis of the project
Then go on explaining the specific tasks that you had to complete
Third, detail the actions that you took in order to deliver the results
And finally, talk about the results of that project.

Using these four steps to frame your answer is the STAR method - as you can see from the initials of each item.

And then you can think of another highlight in your life, doesn’t have to be your greatest achievement, but something that you have strong feelings about, and again, frame it under these four sections: start by describing the situation, then the tasks required to perform, then what actions did you take and finally how the results looked like.

[smile important]
Now, why prepare all these?

You’ll find many great videos on how to answer using this STAR method, but to me, the main thing you’re after here is to prepare a few main stories, highlights, that really define you - because this way, you’re very much likely to be able to associate at least parts of those stories with a given behavioral question, and therefore adequately answer it. 

You can also look-up the most commonly asked behavioral questions {examples in a moment}  and then prepare at least one answer - ideally 2 or three - for each, but to me, having your main stories first is a superior approach.

This is how I see it, and this is how I see the best strategy to bring your A game and avoid some sort of robotic pre-recorded answer; I liked how one applicant who got the job put it: “These interviewers are trained and calibrated to identify crappy people and have an acute attention to bullshit. It’s a quick way to get your candidacy thrown out the window. Just be genuine, show passion for your work, own your flaws, show initiative for improvement and you’ll do fine.”
https://medium.freecodecamp.org/software-engineering-interviews-744380f4f2af 

[smile]
It should go without saying that doing both your main story and answering the most common ones is the ideal thing to do there.

Your personality in order to assess your culture fit overall. One thing you should keep in mind here is this type of assessment is not a disqualifier, except if you’re flagged as trying to impress.

snippet.title: AB INBEV Interview (2 of 3): Hiring process - Trainee Programs (Management, Sales)
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

Looking for someone to role-play before your interview? (free) https://amazoninterview.coach/role-play.php

- Ab inbev hires a lot of trainees using various - and this is one of the most unique aspects of how this company develops in terms of people.

These trainees come from pretty much every corner of the world and the hiring process follows the same pattern, and consists of up to 7 steps:

• Online app


Firts there is an inutial online application that will ask you to ask quite a few questions about you and to make sure that you match the requirements for the program; there are about 10 screens to this process. 


• Online tests


Then the second step is comprised of some online tests - there could be some games and some assessments - such as a personality or logical - with the main objective to assess you as a cultural fit inside AB INBEV and to check your cognitive abilities. There might also be a test to check your English abilities. 

• Video interview


Then there is the video interiew. Apparently it could be either a live interview with a real person or a recorded video interview that will ask you around 10 questions and will record your answers - you have 30 seconds to prepare and then answer each question.

• ABI assessment day


They might ask candidates to prepare a case study on some predefined topic. (examples in the next section).

Overall, this is a one day onsite during which you’ll take part at one of their business games, do some extra interviews and presentation; team work, and getting to know the People at AB InBev.

• Panel interview


The final step is the onsite group panel interview - which is performed by a panel of around 6 people from senior management. So there is a group of candidates that made it through to this step - around 6, and a panel of interviewers asking questions. It takes around one hour.
 
Then if successful there will be an offer.

A. Mission & Ten things we know to be true (Google’s 10 Core Values / Leadership Principles)
1. Focus on the user and all else will follow.
2. It’s best to do one thing really, really well.
3. Fast is better than slow.
4. Democracy on the web works
5. You don’t need to be at your desk to need an answer.
6. You can make money without doing evil.
7. There’s always more information out there.
8. The need for information crosses all borders.
9. You can be serious without a suit.
10. Great just isn’t good enough.

B. Two most important things in a recruit, behavioral questions and how to prepare (STAR method)
Googleyness. The first thing they measure here is cognitive ability, for example, they’ll ask you: Tell me about a tough problem you solved, how did you solve me, walk me through it.
Preparation: 5 stories (full story + shortened into: situation, task, actions, result) + 3 x answers to 20 most common behavioral questions - examples in the video

But one more highlight here in terms of leadership - or at least one more interesting keyword - is emergent leadership. I noticed various Google HR leaders referincing it throughout the years; whta does this mean: it’s essentially your ability to step in when there is a peoblem and step out when they are no linger needed. Would be great if you could also make this stand out in one of your prepared stories.

C. Supercharge your resume with some tips;
Read your CV in 6 seconds. Official advice on structure and more.
And last but not least, and this should go without saying, typos in your resume won’t probably disqualify you, but you can be sure they will have a negative impact, so be sure you triple check it and ideally as a friend to review it for you.

Referrals. Apply through their jobs website. Google’s jobs website is between the very best. Google’s structured hiring is particularly efficient at creating a great applicant experience

So it has been pointed out to me - by someone currently applying for a technical position at AWS - that some of Amazon’s interviews also involve reasoning tests - the numerical reasoning one in particular; the verbal reasoning test according to some online sources, too.

snippet.title: 14 Leadership Principles at Amazon via Jeff Bezos
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

Looking for someone to role-play before your interview? (free) https://amazoninterview.coach/role-play.php

- Amazon Interview Coaching: http://www.amazoninterview.coach/index.html#services Customer Obsession
Leaders start with the customer and work backwards. They work vigorously to earn and keep customer trust. Although leaders pay attention to competitors, they obsess over customers.

Ownership
Leaders are owners. They think long term and don’t sacrifice long-term value for short-term results. They act on behalf of the entire company, beyond just their own team. They never say “that’s not my job". 

Invent and Simplify
Leaders expect and require innovation and invention from their teams and always find ways to simplify. They are externally aware, look for new ideas from everywhere, and are not limited by “not invented here". As we do new things, we accept that we may be misunderstood for long periods of time.

Are Right, A Lot
Leaders are right a lot. They have strong judgment and good instincts. They seek diverse perspectives and work to disconfirm their beliefs.

Learn and Be Curious
Leaders are never done learning and always seek to improve themselves. They are curious about new possibilities and act to explore them.

Hire and Develop the Best
Leaders raise the performance bar with every hire and promotion. They recognize exceptional talent, and willingly move them throughout the organization. Leaders develop leaders and take seriously their role in coaching others. We work on behalf of our people to invent mechanisms for development like Career Choice.

Insist on the Highest Standards
Leaders have relentlessly high standards - many people may think these standards are unreasonably high. Leaders are continually raising the bar and drive their teams to deliver high quality products, services and processes. Leaders ensure that defects do not get sent down the line and that problems are fixed so they stay fixed.

Think Big
Thinking small is a self-fulfilling prophecy. Leaders create and communicate a bold direction that inspires results. They think differently and look around corners for ways to serve customers.

Bias for Action
Speed matters in business. Many decisions and actions are reversible and do not need extensive study. We value calculated risk taking. 

Frugality
Accomplish more with less. Constraints breed resourcefulness, self-sufficiency and invention. There are no extra points for growing headcount, budget size or fixed expense.

Earn Trust
Leaders listen attentively, speak candidly, and treat others respectfully. They are vocally self-critical, even when doing so is awkward or embarrassing. Leaders do not believe their or their team’s body odor smells of perfume. They benchmark themselves and their teams against the best.

Dive Deep
Leaders operate at all levels, stay connected to the details, audit frequently, and are skeptical when metrics and anecdote differ. No task is beneath them.

Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit
Leaders are obligated to respectfully challenge decisions when they disagree, even when doing so is uncomfortable or exhausting. Leaders have conviction and are tenacious. They do not compromise for the sake of social cohesion. Once a decision is determined, they commit wholly.

Deliver Results
Leaders focus on the key inputs for their business and deliver them with the right quality and in a timely fashion. Despite setbacks, they rise to the occasion and never settle.

Long-term profitability is essential to achieving our business goals and to our continued growth. It is a measure both of efficiency and of the value that customers place on Shell products and services. It supplies the necessary corporate resources for the continuing investment that is required to develop and produce future energy supplies to meet customer needs. Without profits and a strong financial foundation, it would not be possible to fulfil our responsibilities. Criteria for investment and divestment decisions include sustainable development considerations (economic, social and environmental) and an appraisal of the risks of the investment.

HEALTH, SAFETY, SECURITY AND THE ENVIRONMENT 
Shell companies have a systematic approach to health, safety, security and environmental management in order to achieve continuous performance improvement. To this end, Shell companies manage these matters as critical business activities, set standards and targets for improvement, and measure, appraise and report performance externally. We continually look for ways to reduce the environmental impact of our operations, products and services.

COMPETITION
Shell companies support free enterprise. We seek to compete fairly and ethically and within the framework of applicable competition laws; we will not prevent others from competing freely with us.

COMMUNICATION AND ENGAGEMENT
Shell companies recognize that regular dialogue and engagement with our stakeholders is essential. We are committed to reporting of our performance by providing full relevant information to legitimately interested parties, subject to any overriding considerations of business confidentiality. In our interactions with employees, business partners and local communities, we seek to listen and respond to them honestly and responsibly.

BUSINESS INTEGRITY
Shell companies insist on honesty, integrity and fairness in all aspects of our business and expect the same in our relationships with all those with whom we do business. The direct or indirect offer, payment, soliciting or acceptance of bribes in any form is unacceptable. Facilitation payments are also bribes and must not be made. Employees must avoid conflicts of interest between their private activities and their part in the conduct of company business. Employees must also declare to their employing company potential conflicts of interest. All business transactions on behalf of a Shell company must be reflected accurately and fairly in the accounts of the company in accordance with established procedures and are subject to audit and disclosure.
+
COMPLIANCE

POLITICAL ACTIVITIES
A. Of companies

Shell companies do not make payments to political parties, organizations or their representatives. Shell companies do not take part in party politics. B. Of employees
Where individuals wish to engage in activities in the community, including standing for election to public office, they will be given the opportunity to do so where this is appropriate in the light of local circumstances.

LOCAL COMMUNITIES
Shell companies aim to be good neighbors by continuously improving the ways in which we contribute directly or indirectly to the general wellbeing of the communities within which we work. snippet.title: 3 Core Values at the New York Times via Mark Thompson
snippet.description:
Upcoming Amazon Telephone Screen? Learn how to answer non-technical questions for $50: https://amazoninterview.coach/#services

- Truth
As journalists we treat our readers, viewers, listeners and online users as fairly and openly as possible. Whatever the medium, we tell our audiences the complete, unvarnished truth as best we can learn it. We correct our errors explicitly as soon as we become aware of them. We do not wait for someone to request a correction. We publish corrections in a prominent and consistent location or broadcast time slot. Staff members who plagiarize or who knowingly or recklessly provide false information for publication betray our fundamental pact with our readers. We do not tolerate such behavior.

Fairness
The goal of The New York Times is to cover the news as impartially as possible — “without fear or favor,” in the words of Adolph Ochs, our patriarch — and to treat readers, news sources, advertisers and others fairly and openly, and to be seen to be doing so. The reputation of The Times rests upon such perceptions, and so do the professional reputations of its staff members. Thus The Times and members of its news department and editorial page staff share an interest in avoiding conflicts of interest or an appearance of a conflict.

Integrity
For more than a century, men and women of The Times have jealously guarded the paper’s integrity. Whatever else we contribute, our first duty is to make sure the integrity of The Times is not blemished during our stewardship.  At a time of growing and even justified public suspicion about the impartiality, accuracy and integrity of some journalists and some journalism, it is imperative that The Times and its staff maintain the highest possible standards to insure that we do nothing that might erode readers’ faith and confidence in our news columns. This means that the journalism we practice daily must be beyond reproach.

Because our voice is loud and far-reaching, The Times recognizes an ethical responsibility to correct all its factual errors, large and small. The paper regrets every error, but it applauds the integrity of a writer who volunteers a correction of his or her own published story. We observe the Newsroom Integrity Statement, promulgated in 1999, which deals with such rudimentary professional practices as the importance of checking facts, the exactness of quotations, the integrity of photographs and our distaste for anonymous sourcing.

Key to success as a leader is to spend more time on making the people on your team successful than you spend on your own.

Particularly philosophical in his speeches, he believes there’s an important connection between being an Employer of choice in an inclusive environment and the engagement of your people from a corporate social responsibility viewpoint.

Their core values blend particularly well with the 4 strategic priorities: professionalism and integrity, quality growth, being an employer of choice and being globally diverse.

The 7 core values at KPMG:

We work together
Bringing out the best in each other and creating strong and successful working relationships.

We respect the individual
Respecting people for who they are and for their knowledge, skills and experience as individuals and team members.

We are open and honest in our communication
Sharing information, insight and advice frequently and constructively and managing tough situations with courage and candor.

We seek the facts and provide insight
Challenging assumptions, pursuing facts, and strengthening our reputation as trusted and objective business advisors.

We lead by example
At all levels acting in a way that exemplifies what we expect of each other and our firms’ clients.

We are committed to our communities
Acting as responsible corporate citizens and broadening our skills, experience, and perspectives through our work in our communities.

Above all, we act with integrity
Constantly striving to uphold the highest professional standards, provide sound advice, and rigorously maintain our independence.


Last but not least, he gives a useful motivational definition for on-boarding / team building purposes: if you have anyone who looks to you over the course of the day for guidance, coaching or feedback, then you’re a leader.

Bonus, here's my full collection of diagrams: https://plus.google.com/+DanCroitor/posts/VpWrDrArBec

The most profound approach in all workplace cultures videos in the series: a CEO openly calling himself the senior pastor of his fifteen thousand strong church - the 3rd largest software company in the world.

The Bible is at the core of the presentation of all the 5 EPIC values:

Execution
Do it Together.

Community
Give more.

Integrity
Build Trust.

Passion
Challenge the Status Quo.

Customers
Make it possible.

The first question coming to my mind was: okay, he is obviously a Christian, but what about diversity? How can a company of that size be on the edge of technology, while being run like a church? 

You’ll have to watch the video for a comprehensive answer - in simple terms, he uses this approach as an glue for their teams, and overall performance; this is for everyone willing to work there, regardless of their religion, willing to abide by their unique dynamics.

And the more I think about this, the more sense it makes – high performing teams often follow  counter-intuitive approaches – the most common example being Amazon’s “two-pizza teams”.

One more thing I found particularly interesting is his approach to mentoring: the one rule he applies to everyone he mentors is that, for the ritual to work, everything must be on the table, “your faith, your family as well as your work, because it isn’t only about making you successful in the workplace but it’s about making you more successful in every aspect of your life”.
